Grace
grayss
noun (the free favour of God)
From the Latin gratia (favour, kindness, thanks), rendering the Greek charis and the Hebrew chen (favour) and chesed (lovingkindness); the unmerited favour of God toward sinners.

See also: Grace

📖 Biblical Definition

Grace is the free and unmerited favour of God toward sinners, the disposition of His heart by which He blesses the undeserving and saves the lost wholly apart from their works. The word translates the Greek charis and answers to the Hebrew chen (favour) and chesed (covenant lovingkindness). Its essence is that it is unearned: where sin abounded, grace did much more abound; and if salvation be by grace, then it is no more of works, otherwise grace is no more grace. The grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared, teaching as well as saving, for grace is not bare pardon but a transforming power. Of Christ's fulness His people receive grace for grace. The Reformed tradition distinguishes uses of the word: common grace, the undeserved kindness by which God restrains evil, sustains the world, and gives rain and fruitful seasons to the just and unjust alike; and saving (special) grace, the effectual favour by which He regenerates, justifies, sanctifies, and glorifies His elect. The dictionary holds grace against two perennial errors. Legalism would mix works with grace, making the favour of God a wage owed to merit; but grace and merit cannot be compounded without destroying grace. Antinomianism would divorce grace from holiness, making it a cloak for sin; but the same grace that saves also teaches the saved to deny ungodliness. True grace is free in its giving and fruitful in its working, the fountain of the whole Christian life from the new birth to glory.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The free, unmerited favour of God toward sinners (Greek charis); distinguished into common grace toward all and saving grace toward the elect; free in its giving, fruitful in its working, opposed alike to legalism and antinomianism.

expand to see more

GRACE, noun. [Latin gratia; Greek charis.] The free and unmerited favour of God toward sinners.

Its essence is that it is unearned: by grace, and not of works (Romans 11:6).

Common grace restrains evil and sustains the world for just and unjust alike.

Saving grace regenerates, justifies, sanctifies, and glorifies the elect.

It is free in giving and fruitful in working, teaching the saved to deny ungodliness (Titus 2:11-12).

📖 Key Scripture

Ro 11:6 — "And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then is it no more work."

Ro 5:20 — "Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound:"

Tit 2:11 — "For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,"

Joh 1:16 — "And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Legalism compounds works with grace until grace is no longer grace; antinomianism divorces grace from holiness and makes it a cloak for sin. The modern “cheap grace” flattens it into mere tolerance.

expand to see more

Legalism, the perennial corruption of grace, mingles works with God's favour, treating salvation as partly earned, so that the sinner contributes his merit and grace fills up the remainder. The apostle declares this impossible: if it be of works, it is no more grace. Rome's system of merit, penance, and the treasury of the saints is the most developed form, but the legalist heart appears wherever a man hopes to commend himself to God by his doing. The dictionary recovers grace as wholly free, lest the cross be made void.

The opposite corruption is antinomian and, in its modern dress, sentimental. “Cheap grace,” in Bonhoeffer's phrase, preaches forgiveness without repentance and acceptance without transformation, until grace becomes a synonym for tolerance and a permission to sin. But the grace of God that brings salvation also teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts. The dictionary holds the two truths the apostle never separated: grace is received by faith alone, apart from all works; and the grace that justifies invariably sanctifies, for it is the power of God unto a holy life and not merely a verdict that leaves the sinner unchanged.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin gratia and the Greek charis (favour freely given), with the Hebrew chen (favour) and chesed (covenant lovingkindness) behind the Old Testament idea.

expand to see more

Charis, Greek, grace, favour freely and undeservedly given.

Chen, Hebrew, favour or graciousness, as “Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.”

Chesed, Hebrew, steadfast covenant love or lovingkindness.

Gratia, Latin, favour, kindness, also thanks, the root of the English word.

“Grace for grace” (John 1:16) names the inexhaustible supply from Christ's fulness.

Usage

"The preacher distinguished common grace, which sends rain on the just and unjust, from the saving grace that regenerates the elect."

"He warned against cheap grace, which preaches pardon without repentance and acceptance without holiness."

"She learned that grace is no wage owed to merit, but the free gift of God she could only receive."
